rule: adjusted_score desc, total_score desc; dedupe by arXiv id / URL / id / title

papers.title: PailitaoMMSearch2.0 Technical Report: Scaling Generative Retrieval to Unified End-to-End Multimodal Search
papers.authors: Xiaohan Ye, Zihan Gong, Jingqian Zhao, Lianyu Du, Yunmeng Shu, Xu Chen, Zesheng Zhou, Renchun You, Bocheng Chen, Jinsong...
papers.summary: In Taobao's Pailitao, a user may photograph a shirt and ask for shorts to match it, which calls for a complementary item rather than a duplicate. The usual pipeline classifies intent first and routes to separate retrieval channels, so one wrong step breaks everything after it. Alibaba's report lets a 2B vision-language model read the raw image and instruction and generate product Semantic IDs directly, with no intent labels. On matching requests the excellent rate rises from 44.2% for the multi-channel pipeline to 74.3%, and online GMV grew 8.94% at full rollout.

papers.title: PinGER: Token-Efficient Generative Retrieval with Semantic IDs
papers.authors: Xinyi Li, Sujan Reddy Ale, Yi-Ping Hsu, Zelun Wang, Yilin Chen, Hanyu Li, Hanlin Lu, Arkin Dharawat, Lulu Yao, Yaxin Li,...
papers.summary: Generative retrieval encodes each item as a multi-level SID and generates it level by level, but on the input side every history item costs several tokens. During training, Pinterest's PinGER places one dense-vector token after each item's SID and requires that any token reading another item may see only that item's dense token, never its SID. At serving time all SIDs in the history can be dropped, each item costs 1 token, and the output is unchanged. ==It turns input compression into a structural constraint at training time==. Offline it matches TIGER's 1,024-token recall with 170 tokens, and after launch on Related Pins saves rose 0.62%.

papers.title: SLIDE: Search-to-List Item Distillation for Single-Rollout Generative Retrieval
papers.authors: Tianyu Zhan, Gui Ling, Ran Tao, Kunhai Lin, Tong Xiong, Wang Yang, Kaixuan Zhang, Zhihong Chen, Yuliang Yan, Dan Ou, She...
papers.summary: Generative retrieval usually produces candidates online with beam search, and the beams never see each other; writing a whole list in one go by greedy decoding is the most direct alternative but works much worse. Taobao's SLIDE (a training method that distills offline search results into lists) moves search offline: a teacher runs beam search for every training request, concatenates the retrieved items in score order into one long sequence, and a student learns it, decoding greedily once online. ==It trades online search cost for offline labeling cost==. With a 7B teacher, the 0.5B student reaches HR@10 of 0.4578, beating the 0.4498 of beam search at the same size.

papers.title: KL-MOPD: Discrepancy-Aware Multi-Objective On-Policy Distillation for Generative Recommendation
papers.authors: Weiqin Yang, Yandong Wang, Yuan Gao, Hao Deng, Jinxin Hu, Jing Cao, Jiawei Chen
papers.summary: When click and value teachers are distilled together into a generative recommender, equal per-token weights are unfair. On TencentGR the student's KL to the value teacher at the first token is 3.13 times its KL to the click teacher, and the harder teacher switches to the click teacher on the last two tokens. KL-MOPD from Zhejiang University and Alibaba weights each teacher per token by its pre-training distance, at no extra training cost. In a 10% traffic online A/B test, ad revenue rose 1.63% and GMV 2.20%.

papers.title: Latent Residual Reasoning for Ranking in Generative Recommendation
papers.authors: Haihan Shi, Ruidong Han, Wenjie Wang, Shangyu Chen, Sunhao Dai, Yongqi Li, Yangyang Li, Fei Jiang, Wei Lin, Fuli Feng, X...
papers.summary: Generative ranking models usually score every candidate in one forward pass. Refiner, from Meituan and the University of Science and Technology of China, adds a few more steps. Each candidate gets a reasoning token, and each step predicts only a correction added to the original score. The base model stays frozen; only LoRA and a new output layer are trained. On Steam it lifts MTGR's AUC from 0.7698 to 0.7872, and a 7-day online A/B behind production MTGR raised CTR by 0.75%. Because it learns only residuals, the extra steps refine the ranking instead of overturning it.

papers.title: MuSID-KD: Multigranularity Knowledge Distillation for Generative Recommendation with Semantic IDs
papers.authors: Fengshi Zhang, Xiyan Ding, Shuxiao Xie, Wei Zhang
papers.summary: When a SID-based generative recommender is distilled into a small model, the student is usually asked only to match the teacher's distribution over which item to recommend in the end. ECNU's MuSID-KD (a multi-granularity distillation method that works level by level over the SID) finds this is not enough: a student aligned only on items disagrees with the teacher on the order of candidate groups at intermediate SID levels in 53.8% of comparisons on average. ==The teacher's knowledge lives not only in the last-level item probabilities but also in the ranking of prefixes at every level==. On three Amazon datasets its NDCG@10 is 8.31% higher on average than basic distillation, with the online inference structure unchanged.

papers.title: From Item Scores to Semantic Tokens: Test-Time Collaborative Adaptation for Generative Recommendation
papers.authors: Xiongfeng Shan, Xing Tang, Hanchong Chen, Fuyuan Lyu, Lingjie Li, Jingyan Jiang, Duguang Liu, Xiuqiang He
papers.summary: In generative recommendation with semantic IDs, the model writes an item's code one token at a time, and beam search keeps only the highest-scoring prefixes at each step. Once a prefix is pruned, every item beneath it can never be generated. The problem is sharpest when a user has just developed a new interest that shows up in only one or two recent interactions. This paper proposes TCBSA (test-time collaborative beam search adaptation), which ==turns a scoring model's item scores into bonuses on code prefixes before every pruning step==. The scoring model scores the whole catalog and keeps the top few hundred items; each item's margin above the cutoff is spread over every step of its code. Before each beam search ranking step, these bonuses are added to the path's cumulative score. Neither model is retrained. Added to TIGER, it raises NDCG@10 by a relative 4.9% to 30.4%, depending on the public dataset. With a narrower beam, it is also more accurate and faster than TIGER with a wider beam.

papers.title: PinRec: Unified Generative Retrieval Model for Pinterest Recommender Systems
papers.authors: Edoardo Botta, Jaewon Yang, Yi-Ping Hsu, Laksh Bhasin, Yilin Chen
papers.summary: Recommender systems usually run a separate retrieval model for the home feed, search and related items, because each surface wants something different: saves on the home feed, outbound clicks to buy on search, and continued browsing on related items. This Pinterest KDD 2026 paper replaces all three with one generative retrieval model, PinRec. It is pretrained on site-wide behavior, fine-tuned on each surface's logs, and told at generation time which action to aim for. ==Conditioning on the target action matters far more than unifying the model==. Removing that condition cuts offline recall on the three surfaces by 7.5% to 12.6%. Added to search as one retrieval source online, it raised saves by 3.88%.

papers.title: JevRec: Linguistic Encoding with Jev-like Decision Modeling for LLM-based Generative Recommendation
papers.authors: Qiyong Zhong, Jiajie Su, Ming Yang, Li Zhang
papers.summary: Most generative recommenders give every item an SID of the same length, so popular items keep paying for fine-grained codes, while shorter codes squeeze long-tail semantics. JevRec borrows the natural-language pattern that frequent words are short: popular items get short SIDs and long-tail items long ones. A dedicated head predicts the length first and a separate head generates content conditioned on it, reducing gradient conflict between the two goals. On three public datasets it beats all compared methods on every metric and trains and infers faster than TIGER.

papers.title: REGER: Modeling inter-item Relations with Semantic IDs for Generative Recommendation
papers.authors: Yuxi Huang, Silin Zhou, Chenhao Wang, Zihan Li, Gangming Guo, Pei Ke, Shen Gao, Shuo Shang
papers.summary: Cross-entropy tells a generative recommender only which token is correct, with no signal about how other candidates compare. REGER, from the University of Electronic Science and Technology of China, splits a conventional sequential model's scores over all items into branch preferences along the SID prefix tree and distills them along the true path. Added alone to TIGER, it lifts Beauty Recall@10 from 0.0673 to 0.0794 with unchanged inference time; removing it from the full model cuts Recall@5 by 10.9% to 18.0%. Two smaller modules add semantic pretraining and attention heads that look at adjacent items.

papers.title: Exploratory creative pre-ranking: Hierarchical empirical-Bayes Thompson sampling for real-time creative optimization
papers.authors: Jiale Han, Ajith Moparthi, Dan Xie, Xiaowu Dai
papers.summary: AI-generated content makes it easy for advertisers to produce many creatives, but each gets very few impressions. This Roblox paper adds a creative pre-ranking layer between recall and ad ranking. The historical play rate μ of a new creative's campaign, game and target audience serves as the prior mean, and the prior strength κ is computed in closed form from the variance of true differences among sibling creatives: the smaller the differences, the larger κ. Adding the creative's own plays and non-plays gives a Beta posterior, and one random score drawn from it is used for ranking. ==Borrowed experience dominates while data is scarce and gives way to the creative's own record as data grows==. On replayed live traffic, it lifts the ranker's predicted play-through rate by 8.14%, against 2.80% for a random shortlist of the same size, the pipeline gets only 0.2% slower, and it now serves production.

papers.title: Hierarchical GTV Estimation: Bridging the Gap between Container-Level Ranking and Item-Level Conversion
papers.authors: Zerong Lan, Fan Zhang, Chuang Chen, Tianchun Huang, Teng Zhang, Xingxing Wang
papers.summary: Local-services and live-commerce ads are ranked and billed per store or livestream room, but users actually buy one voucher or one product inside it, so directly predicting how much a click will sell gives a noisy label that is hard to learn. This Meituan paper splits a store's expected sales into parts: first whether the user orders at all, then each voucher's purchase probability and quantity, multiplied by its price and summed. A store-level regression tower covers samples whose voucher-level signal is too sparse. ==Each sub-task gets a far more stable label==. In a 13-day online A/B test, ad revenue per search rose 1.42%, and the method is fully deployed.

papers.title: iFusion: Integrating Dynamic Interest Streams via Diffusion Model for Click-Through Rate Prediction
papers.authors: Ziheng Ni, Congcong Liu, Yuying Chen, Zhiwei Fang, Changping Peng, Zhangang Lin, Ching Law, Jingping Shao
papers.summary: CTR models usually encode long-term and short-term behavior separately, then concatenate or gate them into one interest vector, so one-off noise in recent behavior, such as stocking up during a sale or buying for someone else, gets written straight into long-term preference. This JD.com ICLR 2026 paper treats long-term interest as a draft: it adds noise, then denoises step by step conditioned on the latest sessions to produce the fused interest vector. ==Each session splits in two: averaging keeps repeated preferences, attention catches sudden interests==, and the stable path gets about twice the weight. In a 7-day online A/B test, CTR rose 2.44% while serving latency grew only about 0.3%.

papers.title: Unified Heterogeneous Feature Interaction via Effective-Rank Scaling for Recommender Systems
papers.authors: Ao Zhang, Haochuan Li, Boya Du, Jian Yang, Qihang Fang, Yulin Xu
papers.summary: Most production ranking models squeeze the user's behavior sequence into one fixed vector before it reaches the feature-interaction module, so later interaction layers can no longer see which clicks or add-to-carts actually happened. Alibaba Taobao's HiRank keeps the behavior sequence alive through every layer of the backbone, and builds the retrieval query over long-term history from the user's recent behavior rather than from static profile fields such as age and gender. On Taobao homepage CVR prediction it lifts GAUC from 0.7615 to 0.7801 over the strongest baseline at the same parameter count; in an online A/B test, orders per user rose 2.27% and GMV per user rose 2.86%.

papers.title: Rethinking Positional Encoding and Interaction Granularity for CTR Prediction
papers.authors: Xinxun Zhang, Yuxiang Wang, Xiaokai Zhou, Jiayue Li, Yi Li, Yue Liu, Jun Zhang, Xiaoling Zhou, Tieyun Qian, Xiao Yan, Ji...
papers.summary: In unified Transformer CTR models like OneTrans, the authors tried six positional encodings on Kuaishou's KuaiRand data, and none beat using no positional encoding at all. Building on this, the Wuhan University and Tencent paper proposes TRIP (the authors' name for the whole method). Each behavior encodes both its rank in the sequence and how long before this prediction it happened. Behaviors are then grouped by that time distance: the seconds before this prediction are put on a base-2 log scale and rounded, so each group spans twice the time of the previous one. Behaviors in the same group see each other, while across groups a behavior sees only earlier groups. ==For the same history, change the impression time and every behavior's distance from now changes==, something language-model positional encodings never had to handle. On four public datasets AUC improves over the strongest baseline by 1.47% relative on average, and by up to 4.45% on the Tencent ad dataset TAAC (a public Tencent ad-click sequence dataset).

papers.title: Towards a Unified Framework of Optimal Input-Side Dimensional Configuration for Deep CTR Prediction
papers.authors: Chaohua Yang, Fuyuan Lyu, Xing Tang, Dugang Liu, Xiuqiang He, Zhong Ming
papers.summary: There are three common ways to trim the input side of a CTR model: drop low-quality training samples, switch off useless features, and prune useless embedding dimensions. Earlier methods do one at a time. This paper from Shenzhen University and collaborators argues that all three are the same operation, multiplying one embedding tensor by a mask at different granularities. They also interact: once a feature is switched off entirely, pruning its dimensions no longer matters. On Avazu with a plain DNN, any single selection raises AUC by only about 0.001. Learning all three together in one model, with penalties that make the levels' decisions fit each other, takes AUC from 0.7893 to 0.7930. Between samples and features, for example, the penalty sums each feature embedding's cosine distance to the sample's average embedding, weighted by the feature gates, and multiplies it by the sample weight. A heavily weighted sample that opens wide gates for outlying features is penalized hard.

papers.title: How Much Fresh Data Should CTR Recalibration Use? A Temporal Evaluation of Post-hoc Calibration
papers.authors: Rui Liu
papers.summary: In ad systems, recalibrating a CTR model on the last few hours of fresh data is usually treated as a routine step that can only help. Testing it day by day on ten days of Avazu ad logs, this paper finds that a calibrator fitted on the first 6 hours of a day makes calibration error worse about a third of the time, and in the worst case doubles it. Stretching the fitting window to the first 12 hours makes this harm essentially disappear. A uniform sample from that span, cut to as few rows as one hour of data holds, does almost as well as the full span and clearly better than using only the latest hour. What decides calibration quality is how much time the data spans, not how many rows it has.

papers.title: MARS: Multi-resolution Adaptive Routing for Sequential Recommendation
papers.authors: Ming Yin, Sixun Dong, Yudong Liu, Wen-Yun Yang, Yunjiang Jiang, Yiran Chen
papers.summary: To save compute, long-history recommenders compress a user's thousands of actions into a small set of cached vectors. This Duke and Meta paper finds that such caches barely remember a user's latest actions while very old ones survive best: ==recent interests get buried under old ones==. MARS writes the history into four memory tracks at once. With each new action, every track fades old content at its own rate: one halves it within a few actions, another only after hundreds. When reading, a small router scores the tracks and each cached vector reads only the top two. On KuaiRec, AUC rises from 0.793 to 0.804, with about 2% more scoring latency.

papers.title: BehaveRec: When Does Long-Term Behavioral History Help Sequential Recommendation? A Study with Session, History, and Community Signals
papers.authors: Aysenur Inan, Reza Yousefi Maragheh, Jayesh Uddhav Kudase, Selene Xu, Kaushiki Nag, Jianpeng Xu, Sushant Kumar
papers.summary: Are long-term history and community signals always useful? BehaveRec's answer is that it depends on how much history a user has. It combines three signals: a causal Transformer over the current session, a bidirectional encoder over 90 days of history, and a user graph built from behavioral similarity, with a gate deciding per user how much of each to use. On industrial data with over ten million users, Recall@5 is 3.2% higher than SASRec, and a larger SASRec still trails, so the gain is not about model size. The more useful result is the stratification: ==users with little history see almost no gain, and the gain grows steadily with history==, with essentially none below about 10 interactions, from which the authors derive a deployment threshold of about 20 interactions. These conclusions hold for category-level intent prediction; the item-level check was a single preliminary run with mixed direction.

papers.title: Can Complementary Signals Bridge Similarity Islands? Manifold-Augmented Graph Embedding for Multimodal Recommendation
papers.authors: Zhenye Yang, Jinpeng Chen, Wenbo Fu, Jun Ma, Huan Li, Qimin Zhou, Tao Wang, Li Sun, Senzhang Wang
papers.summary: Multimodal recommenders often build item graphs from content similarity, so similar substitutes connect tightly while complements that are bought together but look different (a camera and a memory card) stay isolated. MAGE works in two steps. Offline, it splits each item's co-purchased items by text similarity into substitutes and complements. The text vectors of the item and its substitutes form a matrix for SVD; directions with larger singular values represent substitutes more and are removed more strongly. Each complement has its substitute-direction parts removed by these weights, and the averaged residual is added to the item's text vector as a complement direction, with a capped magnitude. Online, image features propagate only over the similar-item graph, augmented text features over the co-purchase graph, and a gate fuses them. ==Pulling complements closer geometrically first keeps propagation from circling only among similar items==. On four Amazon datasets, Recall@20 is about 2.8% to 6.5% higher than the strongest baseline.

papers.title: Semantically Rich, Metrically Affect-Blind: A Geometric Blind Spot in Modern Text Embedders
papers.authors: Mahdi Naser Moghadasi
papers.summary: Search a vector index for what users dislike about a product, and the reviews you get back are usually on topic but a mix of praise and complaints. This paper measures why. Across 11 text embedding models, sentiment is present in the vectors and a simple linear classifier can read it, yet the cosine similarity that retrieval actually uses barely registers it. ==A small projection head on the frozen embedder, trained in seconds on a CPU, repairs this==. It is trained contrastively on a few thousand sentiment-labeled sentences, pulling same-sentiment sentences together and pushing opposite ones apart. When a review sentence is used to find similar sentences, more of those with the same sentiment rank near the top, and the MAP measuring this rises by up to 26 points. The cost is a lower score on the general semantic similarity benchmark STS-B, but after concatenating the head's output with the original vector, it is only 2.4 to 12 points below the original vector.

papers.title: LightRetriever: A LLM-based Text Retrieval Architecture with Extremely Faster Query Inference
papers.authors: Guangyuan Ma, Yongliang Ma, Xuanrui Gou, Zhenpeng Su, Ming Zhou, Songlin Hu
papers.summary: In LLM-based text retrieval, documents can be encoded offline, but queries arrive in real time, so every query runs the full LLM, which keeps throughput low and serving costly. LightRetriever breaks the symmetry: documents still go through the full LLM, while the query side is reduced to a table lookup. During training, a shared prompt plus a single token is fed through the LLM to get that token's vector, and a query vector is the average of its token vectors. ==Every vocabulary token's vector can be precomputed into one table==, so at serving time a query is just lookups and an average. Versus running a full LLM on an A800 GPU, query encoding is over 1000 times faster and end-to-end retrieval throughput rises more than tenfold, while keeping about 95% of the full LLM retriever's retrieval scores on average across benchmarks.

papers.title: System One models Are Not Better Rerankers
papers.authors: Michael Dinzinger, Kanishka Ghosh Dastidar, Michael Granitzer
papers.summary: Using the new decision models to rerank search results does not beat a purpose-tuned reranker, concludes this University of Passau paper. Decision models, also called System One models, answer a question with a calibrated probability of yes instead of text, and within weeks of release they were used for reranking. The paper compares two fine-tunes of the same backbone: decision fine-tuning trains on all kinds of yes-or-no questions to give accurate probabilities, while reranker fine-tuning trains only on MS MARCO queries and passages to judge relevance. Across six Qwen backbones of different sizes and ten TREC DL and BEIR collections, ==reranker fine-tuning wins on every small and mid-sized backbone==, by 5 to 29 points nDCG@10 up to 9B, and the two tie at 27B. Below that size, decision fine-tuning is no better than asking the untuned model. The authors' advice is blunt: if you need a reranker, fine-tune a reranker.

papers.title: EmbeddingGemma 2: Unified and Efficient Multimodal Representations
papers.authors: Henrique Schechter Vera, Sahil Dua, Jovan Andonov, Sara Smoot, Sebastian Russo, Ivan Llanos, Max Matveev, Jae Hyeon Yoo,...
papers.summary: To search text, images, video and audio with one embedding model, the usual route is to transcribe audio and caption images first, then hand everything to a text model. That costs extra compute and throws away tone of voice and visual detail. Google's EmbeddingGemma 2 is a 744M-parameter model that maps these inputs directly into one vector space, and each modality encoder can be loaded only when needed. Finding text passages from a spoken question shows the difference best: the same model transcribing speech to text first reaches an MRR@10 of 57.59, while reading the audio directly reaches 69.54. ==A small multimodal model need not give up text and code==; its code retrieval score is almost ten points above its predecessor's.

papers.title: PersonalQuery-Benchmark:Evaluating Retrieval Robustness to Personalized User Expression Differences
papers.authors: Wenyu Liang, Hongzhi Yin, Tongtong Wu, Fan Liu, Kexin Dai, Weiqing Wang
papers.summary: Two shoppers want the same product. One asks for strawberry, lactose-free Greek yogurt in a short phrase; the other writes a longer sentence and misspells a word along the way. Will search return the same results? This paper builds a benchmark, PQB, from real user reviews in three Amazon categories to test whether results hold up when the same need is worded differently. They often do not. With the core product terms identical and only sentence structure changed, among query pairs where one query puts the target product first, roughly 27% to 52% of the time the other does not. Misspellings that follow the user's own typing habits cut the top-20 hit rate by up to 12.3 percentage points. ==Models with better overall effectiveness are not necessarily more robust==.

papers.title: What the Query Remembers: Query Abstraction Governs Lexical and Dense Retrieval of Classical Arabic Poetry
papers.authors: Omar Farouk Zouak, Selma Mani, Larbi Said Chikh, Raid Abderrezak Ouahioune
papers.summary: When searching a classical Arabic poetry archive, which works better: keyword search with BM25 or an embedding model? This paper finds that the answer depends mainly on how much of the original wording the user still remembers. When users half-remember a few lines, BM25 beats all nine embedding models. When users can only describe what the poem is about, BM25 drops to 8th of 10 systems. ==By rewriting the same queries, the authors show that the ranking is driven by whether the query contains original wording==. Adding half a verse of the original to a query raises BM25 recall by 37.8 points.

papers.title: Closing the Modality Gap via Simplex-Constrained Representations
papers.authors: Shubham Gupta, Siva Reddy, Perouz Taslakian, Valentina Zantedeschi, Cem Subakan
papers.summary: In contrastive models like CLIP and CLAP, the two modalities are trained to align yet their embeddings often sit in offset regions, a phenomenon called the modality gap. This paper leaves the backbone untouched and changes only the space the embeddings live in: the unit sphere is replaced by the probability simplex, where every dimension is nonnegative and all dimensions sum to one. In practice a light softmax adapter is attached to each output, and similarity is computed as total variation distance between the two distributions. ==Both modalities are forced into the same coordinate system, and the offset nearly vanishes==. On five cross-modal retrieval benchmarks, the distance between the modality centroids shrinks by 97% to 99%, with retrieval matching or beating standard models.

papers.title: ACARE: Agent-Context-Aware Reranker for Iterative Search
papers.authors: Sahel Sharifymoghaddam, Yauhen Babakhin, Reza Esfandiarpoor, Oliver Holworthy, Jimmy Lin, Bo Liu
papers.summary: Search agents often send sub-queries of just a few keywords, so a sub-query-only reranker promotes documents that match the words but do not help the real question. ACARe gives the reranker the original question and the agent's reasoning too. The key control: without changing Qwen3-Reranker-4B's weights, adding the question alone lifts a small agent's accuracy from 48.2% to 54.8%, and fine-tuning brings it to 57.6%. Most of the gain comes from the context itself, and all five agents need fewer searches.

papers.title: CA-HNM: Constraint-Aware Hard Negative Mining for Dense Retrieval with Structured Domain Models
papers.authors: Ngoc Luyen Le, Marie-Hélène Abel, Bertrand Laforge
papers.summary: Dense retrievers usually take hard negatives from top-ranked documents that are not labeled positive, but ranking high only shows a document resembles the query, not why it should be excluded. CA-HNM checks each candidate against a course knowledge graph, wrong concept, wrong scope or wrong difficulty level, and keeps only those with a clear conflict as negatives. It beats a rank-matched control without the graph in most settings, yet randomly shuffling the graph on one dataset raises NDCG@10 from 0.0311 to 0.1174, so how much the graph helps is still open.

papers.title: Retriever-Free Retrieval: Navigating Documents with Decision Models
papers.authors: Chao Wan, Paul Jünger, Beixi Du, Bodong Liu, Navaneetha Krishnan, Kilian Q. Weinberger
papers.summary: Most RAG systems still retrieve with BM25 or vector similarity, and evidence the retriever misses cannot be recovered by any generator. DecisionRAG drops the retriever and has a decision model browse like a person in a library, from topics to pages to passages, judging each level's candidates together in one context. Over 2.68 million Wikipedia passages its Hit@1 is 17.4 points above Qwen3-Embedding-8B retrieval plus a reranker, at about 1.7 seconds per query.

papers.title: HiLO: Towards Product-Level Graceful Degradation with a Quality-Aware, Load-Aware Control Framework
papers.authors: Knut Magne Risvik, Zhuowei Li, Nirupam Purushothama, Hunter Su, Greg Dunham, Yan Reznikov
papers.summary: During traffic spikes, each service degrades on its own, so every service survives while the product's quality can collapse. Microsoft's HiLO moves degradation from the service level to the product level. It predefines a few validated product states. Each state sets a level for every service, such as dropping some features, reducing fan-out or using a cheaper model. At runtime services report load and a central controller picks one state. ==The unit of degradation should be the product, not the service==. It went through 9 real traffic surges. The largest hit 2.38 times baseline peak, and Bing's relevance metric OneDCG, a normalized ranking-quality score, dropped at most 0.425 points, inside the 0.5-point operating limit.

papers.title: Cross-Modal Data Co-Locality for Heterogeneous Storage Systems
papers.authors: Abdullah Al-Mamun
papers.summary: A multimodal query first searches text vectors and then fetches the matching image vectors. Both nearest-neighbor searches are fast. The slow part is moving data when the two vectors sit in different storage tiers. CoLoc changes neither the vectors nor the index. It only decides which tier holds what, keeping vectors that are queried together in the same tier. ==It optimizes where data lives, not where to search==. On a four-tier setup, cross-tier queries fell from 73.04% to 0, and end-to-end latency fell 24.8% at a half-multimodal mix, with recall unchanged.

papers.title: Failure-Resilient and Verifiable Distributed Approximate Nearest-Neighbor Retrieval
papers.authors: Abdullah Al-Mamun
papers.summary: Replicas in a distributed vector database keep results available but do not make them trustworthy. A compromised replica can return validly signed but tampered nearest neighbors. TrustANN adds middleware above the router. For each shard it greedily picks a set of replica replies that meets a set minimum size, scores high on pairwise similarity (candidate overlap plus rank agreement), and spans a set number of failure domains such as availability zones. If it falls short, it asks fresh independent replicas, and otherwise returns an explicit unverified status. ==Replicas being online does not make results trustworthy==. In a multi-node test, tampered results accepted as trusted fell from 100% to 0, while p95 latency rose only 9.36% under normal load.

papers.title: Folding Attention Biases into Keys Makes Compacted KV Caches Run on Standard Kernels
papers.authors: Utkarsh Kanwat
papers.summary: KV cache compression can already cut a long document's cache to a tenth, but the strongest method, Attention Matching, adds a bias to every kept key, and vLLM has no slot for it. Using the queries produced while reading the document, this paper computes one direction per attention head on which those queries project to 1 on average, then moves each key along it by the bias times a fixed factor. Queries whose projection is close to 1 then see a score change about equal to the bias, leaving an ordinary KV cache. Unmodified vLLM on one T4 fits 31 concurrent requests instead of 4.

papers.title: Let the Gate Decide: Per-Lookup Precision for Quantized Conditional Memory in LLMs
papers.authors: Tianqi Chen, Xunchao Li, Linchuan Xie, Guanghua Yu, Jianchen Zhu, Peisong Wang, Jian Cheng
papers.summary: When you quantize a language model's n-gram memory tables to low bits, keeping the most frequently accessed rows precise does worse than picking rows at random. The reason is the gate. In conditional memory layers such as DeepSeek's Engram, each fetched vector is scaled by a gate; common function words get small gates, rare entity names get large ones, and quantization error is scaled by the gate. GateRQ stores each row as a few levels of 1-bit residual codes and reads level 1 to compute the gate. It then ranks lookups within the batch by gate-based importance: the top few read to level 3, the next ones to level 2, and the rest stop at level 1. The share at each level is fixed by a preset budget of average bits read per lookup. Without retraining, it cuts DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash's table memory from 23.6 GiB to 3.0 GiB per GPU, and the freed memory clearly raises long-context throughput over FP8 tables.

papers.title: WAKMan: Workload Aware KVCache Manager
papers.authors: Suhas Kumar Morisetty, Vaibhavi Lokegaonkar, Sachin Mathew Varghese, Wesley Harris
papers.summary: Which eviction policy vLLM's prefix cache should use depends on the traffic arriving right now. Agent requests come back within seconds with the same history, so the default LRU fits. Popular system prompts and long chat histories return much later, and only S3FIFO, which protects blocks used repeatedly, keeps them. Across 20 request mixes, each policy wins some. WAKMan replays the traffic of the last 15 minutes on two simulated caches and uses whichever had the higher hit rate for the next window, gaining 5 points of hit rate over LRU alone on average.

papers.title: BellowsKV: One Latent for Many Layers, Expanded on Demand
papers.authors: Jiamu Zhang, Hanjie Chen
papers.summary: In long-context inference, the largest memory cost is often the per-layer KV cache, the keys and values attention stores for every past token. BellowsKV observes that caches of adjacent layers differ, but the hidden states that produce them are similar. So it shares the input, not the cache. For each token, it concatenates the hidden states of n adjacent layers and multiplies them by a compression matrix, giving one shared vector that replaces those layers' caches. Each layer has its own restore matrix that maps the shared vector back to its keys and values. Both are solved once offline from calibration data to minimize reconstruction error, with no training. ==Share the input, not the cache==. On 3 models it keeps over 97% of accuracy at about 14x compression, with decoding speed close to uncompressed.

papers.title: Where Rounding Happens Matters: Rounding-Location Alignment Stabilizes LLM Reinforcement Learning
papers.authors: Yijing Ke, Tianle Cai, Ruosong Wang
papers.summary: LLM reinforcement learning usually generates answers with one inference engine and trains with another framework. Even with identical weights and BF16 on both sides, the numbers differ slightly, so an update meant to be on-policy quietly becomes off-policy and training can suddenly collapse. This paper from ByteDance Seed and Peking University finds that the two systems need not be aligned wholesale. It is enough to round at the same place on both sides in three spots, RoPE, SwiGLU and residual RMSNorm, keeping those intermediates in FP32 until their BF16 outputs. ==With all three aligned, four Qwen-family models no longer collapse==, and aligning RoPE alone also suffices. The inference engine, matmul and attention kernels, and the training objective stay unchanged.

papers.title: KVStream: Adaptive Parallel Storage Management for KV Caching in Large-Scale LLM Serving
papers.authors: Avinash Maurya, Jaiaid Mobin, Jie Ye, M. Mustafa Rafique, Franck Cappello, Bogdan Nicolae
papers.summary: Long-context inference keeps reusing the same prefixes: system prompts, whole documents, code repositories and multi-turn session histories. Their KV cache no longer fits in GPU memory or host memory, so it has to live on disk and be read back on the next hit, which puts disk reads on the critical path of every inference step. Existing systems read only from the node-local NVMe, while the parallel file system that every cluster already mounts sits almost idle. This paper builds KVStream: every KV chunk is written to both the local disk and the shared storage. ==At read time both tiers read at once, and whichever finishes first claims the next batch==. Plugged into LMCache, it reaches up to 1.49x LMCache's offline throughput and up to 6.1x lower mean TTFT under bursty traffic.

papers.title: C 2 KV: Compressed and Composable KV Cache Reuse for Efficient LLM Inference
papers.authors: Chuheng Du, Junyi Chen, Hanlin Tang, Kan Liu, Tao Lan
papers.summary: Retrieval-augmented generation stitches several retrieved documents into the context, and recomputing their KV caches from scratch every time is expensive, so some methods store each document's KV cache and concatenate them on use. But long documents have huge KV caches, so storing and loading them becomes the bottleneck, and naively compressing them before concatenation hurts accuracy badly. This paper from Shanghai Jiao Tong University and Alibaba proposes C2KV: a light extractor beside the frozen model reads each document followed by a few learnable compression tokens and keeps only those tokens' KV as the document's cache. ==Caches are stored without positions, which are re-applied at concatenation time==, so they combine like building blocks. On long contexts, inference is up to 17 times faster with generation quality largely preserved.

papers.title: OXE-AugE: A Large-Scale Robot Augmentation of OXE for Scaling Cross-Embodiment Policy Learning
papers.authors: Guanhua Ji, Harsha Polavaram, Lawrence Yunliang Chen, Sandeep Bajamahal, Zehan Ma, Simeon Adebola, Chenfeng Xu, Ken Gold...
papers.summary: Generalist robot policies must control many arm and gripper combinations, but recollecting data and retraining for each new robot is too costly. The widely used Open X-Embodiment dataset gathers over sixty robot datasets yet is badly imbalanced: the top four robot types make up over 85% of its real data. This paper builds an augmentation toolkit that extends existing demonstrations to nine other arm and gripper combinations, yielding OXE-AugE with 4.4 million trajectories, more than three times the original. The abstract gives the scale and findings but not how actions are converted to the new robots. Experiments show ==diverse robot augmentation helps not only the augmented robots== but also unseen robots and the original robots under distribution shift.

papers.title: Coupling Execution Horizon and Sampling Depth in Flow-Matching VLA Policies
papers.authors: Jiabing Yang, Yuan Xu, Yixiang Chen, Qisen Ma, Peiyan Li, Kai Wang, Chenhang Cui, Tao Yu, Zichen Wen, Wen Ye, Bowen Fang...
papers.summary: In flow-matching vision-language-action models, solver steps and execution horizon turn out to be coupled, and the best setting can reverse. These models start from random noise and use a numerical solver to push it step by step into a smooth action chunk. Deployment usually tunes the two separately: the horizon amortizes inference latency, while solver steps stay high for accuracy. Under frequent replanning, fewer solver steps do hurt, but ==when a long stretch of actions runs open loop, fewer solver steps actually help==, because coarse integration keeps actions closer to the mean trajectory and limits compounding drift. Executing 5 actions at a time, 10 solver steps win. Executing 20 at a time, 2 solver steps win. The pattern holds across benchmarks and real robots, cutting latency and raising success without training.

papers.title: FLORA: An Open Model Suite for Scaling Robotics Data Engines
papers.authors: Sicong Leng, Yunze Man, Zhiqi Li, Jing Wang, Yuhe Zhang, Ryan Punamiya, Siddharth Patki, Kaiyuan Zheng, Zi-ang Cao, Zhid...
papers.summary: Training robot foundation models takes huge amounts of labels: deployments need task-success judgments, reinforcement-learning post-training needs per-step process scores, and pretraining needs timestamped captions to filter data. NVIDIA has open-sourced Flora, the data engine used to train GR00T, where ==one model produces all three kinds of labels==. It sets the best scores on public captioning and reward benchmarks and matches GPT-6 Astra on internal tests. It is roughly 125 times cheaper and labels 200,000 hours of data a day on 512 GB300s.

papers.title: OpenJaws: An Open Hardware UMI Framework with Stereo Localization for Generalist Manipulation
papers.authors: Adithyavairavan Murali, Yash Oza, Karanbir Chahal, Neel Jawale, Silas De Vries, Hesam Rabeti, Erwin Coumans, Balakumar S...
papers.summary: Collecting robot demonstrations in the wild with a handheld gripper (UMI) is now common, but how good the action labels are depends on one step: recovering the gripper trajectory from the wrist-camera video. The original UMI uses a monocular camera plus an IMU (inertial measurement unit); a single camera cannot see true scale, so it also needs a pre-built map and a fiducial marker to stay stable. OpenJaws swaps in a stereo camera that costs about a hundred dollars. The distance between the two lenses is calibrated, so triangulation gives true scale directly. On a new benchmark with ground truth, comparing only segments both methods can track, the stereo trajectory error is about 2.9 mm versus 18.4 mm for the original pipeline, which also tracks only 37% of frames on average. The whole gripper costs about $400, and all hardware and software are open source.

papers.title: Pushing Dexterity and Safety for In-Hand Object Pose Reaching That Works Remarkably Well
papers.authors: Ian Chuang, Hiya Shah, Vamsi Chilamkur, Iman Soltani, Claire Tomlin
papers.summary: Skills learned by multi-fingered hands mostly stop at simple grasps or spinning an object in place. For harder in-hand moves the most common failure is dropping the object, yet earlier work rarely counts drops. This paper has a LEAP hand move a held object to almost any position and orientation, with random wrist orientations, through one goal after another. The main policy is trained entirely in simulation and transfers directly to the real hand. On the real hand it accurately reaches 95.2% of unseen goals. The authors then stack a small network on the frozen main policy. Seeing only the hand and object state, it learns with reinforcement learning to add a small correction to each action, rewarded for keeping the object and for keeping corrections small. The penalty weight on corrections can be set at run time, and a larger weight keeps actions closer to the original. Drops fall by 75% while 91.5% of goals are still reached.

papers.title: Zero-HLM: Generalizable Humanoid Loco-Manipulation without Real Robot Data
papers.authors: Dianyi Yang, Mengya Liu, Zhumei Wang, Yu Liu, Xiaochen Zhang, Yixuan Li, Le Ma, Yuhang Yang, Weiqi Huang, Wei Liang, Bao...
papers.summary: Teaching a humanoid a long task such as walking to a table, picking up a banana and putting it in a basket usually takes a hundred or more teleoperated real-robot demonstrations, and moving the table often means collecting them again. Zero-HLM builds all of its data in simulation instead. It scans a real room with a smartphone, rebuilds it as a simulated scene that looks like a photo and supports physical interaction, and rewrites a few teleoperated demonstrations into a thousand or more new ones. Each new demonstration randomly moves the robot's starting point and the positions of the object and placement target, the hand trajectory moves along with the target, and only those that succeed in simulation are kept. A policy trained only on this data and deployed on the real robot averages 66.7% success over three tasks, above the 46.7% from training on real demonstrations. At positions the real demonstrations never covered, success rises from 23% to 69%.

papers.title: DiscoDemo: Discovering Efficient and Diverse Robot Demonstrations for Imitation Learning
papers.authors: Minho Park, Kinam Kim, Donghu Kim, Byungkun Lee, Dongyoon Hwang, Yongjae Shin, Junha Hyung, Hojoon Lee, Jaegul Choo
papers.summary: Imitation learning depends heavily on how widely its demonstrations cover the task, but collecting diverse successful demonstrations is expensive. This paper ==uses reinforcement learning as a data generator rather than a deployable controller==. DiscoDemo trains a generator where each latent code yields a different way to solve the task; training starts from states near the goal and gradually backs off. A diversity reward grows as the states visited under different latent codes lie farther apart in a learned representation, and it is given only to trajectories that complete the task. The generator's trajectories are filtered: failures are dropped, then any with unwanted robot-scene contact or excessive insertion force; the rest become a static dataset for a downstream visuomotor policy. Across four manipulation tasks, average downstream success versus the strongest baseline rises from 40% to 62% in simulation. On the real robot it rises from 39% to 78%.

papers.title: GRAFT: Geometry-Aware Residual Adaptation for Foundation Trackers
papers.authors: Liang Li, Guoyao Zhang, Xingyu Chen, Sikai Wu, Qianyang Wu, Yuhang Lin, Renjing Xu, Mingliang Zhou, Diyun Xiang
papers.summary: Humanoid behavior foundation models (BFMs, general tracking policies that turn a reference motion into whole-body joint commands) are mostly trained on flat-ground motion and tend to fall on stairs, gaps and platforms. The usual fix is to retrain or fine-tune the whole model together with perception, which is costly and can damage what it already does well on flat ground. Xiaomi Robotics Lab's GRAFT freezes the foundation model completely and adds only a small adapter that applies terrain-dependent corrections to lower-body execution targets, with corrections pushed close to zero on flat ground. Four frozen foundation models could barely cross the hardest terrain; with GRAFT, the best one goes from 3 successes out of 40 to 39. Using only an onboard depth camera, the adapter also runs on a real Unitree humanoid.

papers.title: PlayPolicy: Dexterity from Supervised Play
papers.authors: Botao He, Yiming Dou, Yiannis Aloimonos, Jitendra Malik, Akash Sharma, Ruoshi Liu
papers.summary: To learn to push objects or turn an object in hand to any pose, a dexterous hand usually needs either demonstrations for each task or reinforcement learning in simulation followed by transfer to the real robot. PlayPolicy, from Amazon FAR and collaborators, has a person teleoperate the hand to fiddle freely with objects for a few minutes, and uses behavior cloning to learn a play policy tied to no task. The robot then plays on its own for hours, and this data trains a world model that predicts what actions will do. For a specific goal, the play policy proposes candidate actions, the world model predicts each outcome, and the one closest to the goal is executed. On the real robot its success rate is 69.6% higher than behavior cloning with goals relabeled afterwards, and it matches reinforcement learning with about 490 times less interaction data.

papers.title: BitVLA: 1-bit Vision-Language-Action Models for Robotics Manipulation
papers.authors: Hongyu Wang, Chuyan Xiong, Ruiping Wang, Xilin CHEN
papers.summary: Vision-language-action models are too large for the edge devices robots carry. Rather than compressing after training, BitVLA uses extreme low-bit weights from the start: every parameter is one of minus one, zero or one, about 1.58 bits, conventionally called a 1-bit model, built on the open BitNet LLM. The vision encoder's weights are quantized to the same three values, and training pulls its image representations toward those of the original full-precision encoder. ==It matches the full-precision OpenVLA-OFT baseline== while cutting model memory by 11 times and end-to-end latency by 4.4 times.
